utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution together with my colleagues, April Carter, and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We trust that everyone had a good weekend. The sun actually broke through the grey this weekend, which was kind of nice. This morning there is Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Chad Mair, Daniela Tasic, Novak Lukic, and I am Gregor Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. The Prosecution, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Carter will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Lieutenant-Colonel Per Anton Brennskag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you think you can spell out his names while we're waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The first name is P-e-r, second name A-n-t-o-n.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if everyone's hearing this, but I'm getting French out of everyone channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What channel are you on?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have run one through 1, 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. You've got to stay on 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm still hearing French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why am I not hearing French? I'm on 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we could have Madam Carter helped, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I can use the secondary set of.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Are you okay now, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I will use the secondary set of microphones and earphones for ease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Brennskag, can you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Per Brennskag. I am 60 years old, and I'm from Norway. I'm a retired army man, retired from the Norwegian army, since 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the name Anton fit anywhere in your names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the name, Anton fit anywhere among your names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Per Anton Brennskag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you've indicated that are you an army man. Can you please tell us, when did you enter the Norwegian army?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I entered the officer course in the Norwegian army as an infantry man in 1970, and I graduated from the Military Academy in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You've indicated that you were in an infantry officer. Can you please tell the Court what type of training that you received, in order to hold such a position.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I had my basic training as an infantry officer from 1970. I was introduced with the rifles, the normal infantryman use and other weapons we used. We were educated how to use the terrain, how to patrol, how to lead a squad and so on; and afterwards, during my whole career, I was -- learned to -- how to plan, how to prepare, and how to execute, for example, attacks on ground, and how to use the - what should I say? - okay, I stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarity for the record, you were having difficulty choosing the last word. Is it accurate that English is not your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: My English is not my mother tongue, and it's seldom I am using English now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. But are you comfortable using the English language in court today?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I try my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we can ask. Sir, at some point in time did you begin to work for the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Please say again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some point in time did you begin working with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, I attended an UN observer course in Finland. It's an operational course, lasted three or four weeks, preparing officers for the job as unarmed observers, especially for the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, specifically, what type of training and education did you receive in order to become an unarmed observer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was both practical and theoretical. The theory was to cope with military English, of course, the history, especially, about Middle East, and the politics in the Middle East. The practice was very good. It was how to observe from an observer post, how to make patrols, how to behave in the case you were hijacked, how to cope with a car that was wrecked, how to repair it, and how to drive in very difficult terrain, and how to work together with other observers from other countries. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you take this education and training that you received and use it in the field?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. During the course, we were very much in the field to practice this. For example, we were very realistical [sic] hijacked, stripped from clothes, and had to go back to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After you received this training, did you become an UN military observer in the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I went down to the Middle East in - I think it was in June - the same year, in 1992, and I was an unarmed observer half a year on the demarcation line between Lebanon and Israel and the last half year in Syria, on Golan.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After your service in the Middle East, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Then, of course, I went back to my job in the army in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you later called upon to be an UN observer again?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I applied for it, and in early 1988 I was a little bit surprisingly asked to go to Balkans as an unarmed military observer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You gave the year to go to the Balkans as 1988; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you give the clarify the year?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And when you entered the Balkans in 1995, what was your original assignment?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In the UN observer team, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, my assignment was to be an unarmed military observer, and I was -- my first posting was in what we call Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In that first Sector Sarajevo posting, which division or portion of Sector Sarajevo were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I was assigned to the observer team in Pale on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you stay the entire time in Pale or did you later move on to another division?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, I didn't stay the entire time. I was luckily enough to get out of Pale the 24th of May for a leave, and I think it was the 25th or 26th, the first NATO air-strike, and all my colleagues were seized or detained, so I never could go back to Pale, so after my leave, I was posted inside Sarajevo on the Bosnian -- BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where were you specifically posted within Sector Sarajevo, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At first, I were posted in an observer team which we called Team Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Within Team Pofalici, did you also man an observation post?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. The Team Pofalici had an observation post on the hillside called Vitkovac it's just east of Rajlovac radio station on the hillside and north of -- a little bit north of the new town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, did that observation post correspond to a number?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was called 4, OP 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. After your service as a military observer within the Pofalici team, did you remain in that status or did you take another responsibility within the UN sometime thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not really sure of the date, but sometimes in the middle of August, I was asked to be a liaison officer inside Sarajevo to liaise between UN observer HQ in Sarajevo, and the police in Sarajevo, and the military units inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, when did you depart Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Excuse me. I departed Sarajevo, I think it must be the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now that we have established your biography, I would like to focus a bit more on your work within Sarajevo. First, I would like to move a general description before we get into the specifics that you participated there in Sector Sarajevo. Can you please describe the role and the responsibilities as an unarmed observer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. The unarmed observers inside Sarajevo had normally the job to observe from observer posts. They should, of course, patrol areas, but normally we were very restricted. We had to investigate accidents or -- what could I say, what something happened, impacts, wounded people, killed people. You had to investigate and make reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you were observing. What specific were you observing?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We were observing military movements but mostly impacts inside Sarajevo and outgoing mostly mortars from Sarajevo and out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say that you were observing mostly impacts inside Sarajevo, what was impacting Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Mostly impacts inside Sarajevo was from artillery and mortars and also what is known as modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of who was firing this artillery, mortars, and air bombs?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the times, we could see from where it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And predominantly where was this firing coming from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The firing into Sarajevo were -- excuse me, do you mean from which area?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, who was firing it.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Mostly, the firing with artillery and mortars and modified air bombs was fired from BSA-held areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please indicate to the Court what does BSA stand for?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: For me, the Bosnian Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, based on your observations, did you learn where the confrontation lines were therein Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The confrontation line differed sometimes because of the fightings, but, in brief, we knew every time where the confrontation line was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to bring up 65 ter 4448. And I will be asking the witness to identify the confrontation lines by marking on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we getting the 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: 65 ter 4448 is a street map of the entirety of Sarajevo, and the Prosecution would seek to admit the clean copy into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P540. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now with the assistance of the usher, I would like you to identify for the Court the confrontation lines that were in place in summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Excuse me, it's very long time ago, 1995, and it's very small figures on the map, so I ask to -- could use a help map, my private map, to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'd like that -- to have the opportunity to review this gentleman's private map before he uses it, so I know what it has on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For ease of the Defence counsel, it actually is the final page of the 2006 statement, which is a highlighted -- or a much more -- less detailed map than the one that we have present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that understanding, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're sure you don't want to see what the gentleman has.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to see it just to verify it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the usher to please tender the copy to Defence counsel prior to him using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, I guess you are aware that the Bench doesn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. This is neither a 65 ter listing nor is it going to be entered into evidence. It's merely the back page and the witness's own private map that he has created, but we're using the official map that is present on the screen for the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm happy to provide a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I -- if I might, can ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I believe that it was the same map. We can certainly put on the ELMO, so the Court can see it so we know what he is marking off the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could -- to make life easier if Carmela can just take a look at the map that she has in her hands because it is not what I have right here, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can have the usher give the black and white copy, the final page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, the map the gentleman has indicated is the map that he wishes to uses is not the same map that we have been supplied. I'm going to hand both maps to the usher so that Ms. Carter can review them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I do stand corrected. The map that the gentleman does have in his possession currently is more detailed. However, again, he is merely using it as an aide-memoire to be able to mark the confrontation lines on the official map. Again, we can certainly use the ELMO so we can all be aware of what he is reviewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If somebody would do my the kindness of running me a copy of the map so that have it available, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That can certainly be done. If we can have just a moment. I don't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, do I read from what you are saying, that you don't mind the map being used. As long as you have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As long as I have a copy. If it is of assistance to the witness in terms of his testimony, I have no objection whatsoever to it being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Am I to understand that we can use it currently but as long as we provided it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And also just so we're clear, on the record, that the map that has been supplied in the gentleman's 2006 statement is not the map; and perhaps we can inquire as to when this map was produced so we have some indication and understanding of the provenance of this particular map apart from the fact that he made it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That would have to come from the witness himself because it not in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the coloured map that you brought into court today, where does that map come from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This map is made on me for private reasons, to remember the observation posts and to remember approximately confrontation lines. And it's made, I'm not sure, but long before 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that you yourself made this map. Did you keep it in your private collections?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the coloured map can be provided back to the witness. And I believe that answers Mr. Guy-Smith's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, sir, using your aide-memoire, if you please mark on the official map the confrontation lines that were present in Sarajevo in 1995.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll try. Anyhow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness indicated earlier that the map on the screen is too small. Can we zoom in a little bit for him to see what he wants to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we zoom in, we won't be able to see the full confrontation line, and the witness did see the same map yesterday in a black and white form. It takes us a little while, but we'll get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You go ahead, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not very sure where Grbavica is on this map, but BSA-held Grbavica. Then I have tried to mark the confrontation line as good as I can see the map. But, anyhow, it's very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you indicate for the Court within the figure that you drew who held that territory?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Excuse me. I try to explain the airport was so-called neutral area held by UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And can you please indicate on that drawing, just write the word "airport" in English to designate that area.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You've used two acronyms, BSA and ABiH. Can you please indicate for the Court what they stand for?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: BSA, for me, Bosnian Serb held area. ABiH, army BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would request a screen-shot of this exhibit, and we tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given exhibit P541. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can now have a clear copy again of P540, highlighting the grid markings D, E, and F, at 3 and 4. If we can narrow down on the top left corner a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Brennskag, on the map before you, can you identify the location of the Pofalici team an observation post number 4?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If could you please identify where observation post 4 is located on this map, with the numeral 4, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I see that you've placed a triangle next to the number 4. Are you indicating that where the triangle is located is where observation post 4 is located?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As accurate as is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you remain on observation post 4 the entire time, or was the remainder of your team located somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The team was located in a hired building in -- in -- and it was only two, at the time, at the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. If you can please mark with a square where the remainder of the team was when they were not on post?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Somewhere where I marked the circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. So where the circle is, is where the remainder of the team was, and where the triangle is, is where the observation post 4 is; is that correct for the record?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd ask for a screen shot of this map and tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be given Exhibit P542. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And thank you to the usher, and I believe that will be the last thing we'll be marking for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you touched on this briefly when discussing the map itself, but I'd like to talk a little bit further about a Pofalici team. Can you please tell me, how many people were on this team?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It differed. It could be nine, or it could be seven. It depended because someone was always going out from the team and someone was always coming in. Old ones going out and new ones coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you indicated that at time there is was a separation between two people who were on the observation post and the remainder who stayed behind. I'd like to focus first on the people who were left behind, not on post. What was their job during the day?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Their job were to investigate. Their job were to patrol. And their job were to have contact with officials, let's say, health department, UN observer HQ, and also have some internal administration job.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated at times they were serving to investigate. What were they investigating and how were they being called out to investigate?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Let's say if it was an impact inside Sarajevo, we were called out by the UN observer HQ to investigate the -- the site and also to check if there were some wounded. Sometimes we had to go to the hospital to see the wounded or even go to see the dead ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now moving on to the second job. You indicated at times they were patrolling. What area was the Pofalici team patrolling and how did they choose that area?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The patrolling was decided from the UN observer HQ inside Sarajevo, but as I said, it was fairly a few patrolling because of the restrictions of movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the remainder of the positions, how did people get chosen for those positions?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that others -- their job was to have contact with officials such as the health department, the UN observer HQ and some having internal administration jobs. How were people selected for those positions?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We were always having a team leader, normally the most senior officer, or he was normally chosen as a team leader from the UNMO or the UN observer HQ.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were selected for one of those positions did you remain in that position the entire time you were in the Pofalici team or did you alternate between those positions?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I was not team leader during my time in the Pofalici team.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, I'm speaking more if he were chosen to patrol or to investigate or to do any of those roles, did you do that the entire time or was it on a case-specific basis?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I did all the jobs on specific basis when I was told to do the patrolling, told to investigate or going to the OP. I did all the job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. Now we'll move to the OP itself. You indicated before that two persons served at the observation post at a time. Can you please describe how the two people were selected to go to the observation post per day?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: There were certainly a turn-around list, so everyone had to go to the observer post. Two people were there 24 hours a time, and then we changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were the two people who served together, were they people who always served in pairs or did the teams, themselves, alternate as well?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: These alternated. I didn't say that in the team there were no people from -- no officers from the same nation in same team, and we tried to alternate who was working together also in the OP and also for the investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where specifically was this observation post, in what type of structure?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was a normal living house what was hired. The two elderly couple who owned it, they placed themselves in the basement to be safe, and we hired the ground floor, and the first floor where they had a sleeping room, and on the balcony we had a -- on the balcony, we had the binoculars to observe.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where could you observe from that location?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We could observe Igman, the Igman mountain, to the west; the airport; Hrasnica; south-east -- south-west of the airport; we could observe the hills overlooking Sarajevo eastwards towards Grbavica; just downhill to the west, we couldn't see the old airport Rajlovac air field, but we could see a part of the railway line going to Rajlovac railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You've indicated some areas such as eastwards towards Grbavica and that type of thing. Just for ease of the record, what locations did that -- that include?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can you tell me, from that observation post, were you able to see the hills of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The hills above Dobrinja, yes, north of Dobrinja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you able to see the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the south-east of the airport not far away from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you also able to see Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were on post, I want to talk specifically about your work while serving there. You had touched on before that you were seeing a lot of incoming fire from the Bosnian Serb army into Sarajevo. Can you please tell me what type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is not precisely accurate. He had seen a lot of incoming fire. It's a bit expansive.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what were you primarily seeing from observation post 4? Who was firing and where were they firing?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We can see who was firing. We could see -- or mostly who was firing, from where it was firing. We could see the impacts inside Sarajevo from weapon -- weapons who were -- who were used. That were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With specificity, what were you predominantly seeing in observation post 4? Who was firing and what were they firing?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I saw both parties firing, but mostly the firing was incoming into Sarajevo from BSA-held side. We could also observe ABiH firing from inside Sarajevo, mostly with -- from mortars, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If you can tell me --

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Excuse me. But we could -- had problems to see the impacts from the mortars fired from ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that you were seeing mostly the firing from the BSA-held side. What were they firing?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: They were firing artillery rounds, mortar rounds, modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How often did you see incoming artillery rounds and mortar rounds?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In June, it was a very hectical [sic] time, and it could be up to 150 impacts incoming and impacts inside Sarajevo during 24 hours, sometimes, and it differed. But most it could be up to 150.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were these 150 rounds hitting civilian targets, military targets, both or neither?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In my view, both. Some of the impacts was obviously because of the fighting between the parties, but some rounds were not impacting like this, impacting -- and it was civilian targets in my view, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What do you base this opinion on?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Because it could be single rounds and no -- at my knowledge, up to now, no military targets, and we investigated the impacts, the team or another team, and it was purely civilian wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When an incoming round was being sighted, how was the observation post able to register or log these things?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We were always two to agree what we saw and heard. If we didn't agree, we didn't report. In this way, we were able to fairly accurate point out the grids where the impact was -- where impact was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once agreement was reached, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We wrote it down, and normally we reported by radio to the UNMO HQ in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did you -- you said you reported it by radio normally. Why only normally and why not always?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Because of our safety. We used normal radio with no codes or very few codes, and we reported the grids of the impact from artillery; and, of course, everyone was listening. And the -- in my military view, we were sometimes observation post for the artillery of the -- from the BSA side. And obviously the ABiH didn't like that. So they started to fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What do you mean that you were sometimes an observation post for the artillery fire of the BSA?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: To be accurate, at the ground, you need an observation post to correct the first rounds or impact to hit the place you are supposed to hit. If I can -- it's a bad explanation, but ... Can I -- an artillery -- from where you fired an artillery, you normally can't see the -- the goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if you can't see the goal, what do you do to correct that, if you didn't hit it?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Then the observation post call back to the artillery and tell them how to correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you indicating that the UN called back the BSA and told them how to correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. Our intention was to mark or -- and send the grid where the impact actually was, and the BSA, of course, they were listening and then they could correct where to fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to focus a little bit more about your communications with the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would like to bring up 65 ter 8594.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This document is a daily report made by the UNMO HQ to be sent to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you please tell us what days events are being recorded in the situation report?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In this situation report, everything that is reported from the observation posts and from the patrols and from the investigations is put down in a daily report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If can you clarify for us, I know the report is dated on the 19th, but the subject line reads that it is referring to the 18th of June, 1995. Which days events are being recorded?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's the 18th that is reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now like to move to page 7 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to note down at the bottom where it's talking about the ceasefire violations and firing incidents, if you can please explain to the Court what each of the columns represent in this?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I try. The column to the left is the date and the time the incident happened; and it's time is local time. That's why the Bravo is put behind the time. Then the next column is from where and who is reporting. Let's say line number 2 is stated OP 4. It was my observation post and you also see the map grid behind the -- from where the report is sent. The third column is what happened. I still used the line 2, for example, 13 explosions. Then column 4 is the origin of fire, from where the fire was coming; and I use an example here, the line 2 again, unknown, because here, then obviously OP 4, they didn't know exactly from where the origin of fire. Then the next column, impact target area, there is noted where the impact was observed with a grid, example again, line 2. It's stated that the impact, the 13 explosions, were impacted in Nedzarici; and you have a map grid on that. And the last column, remarks, and in my example, line 2, it is nothing in line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't understand the first few columns. If the witness could please explain them reading what is written there. He didn't do so. He started reading what is written there when he talked about 13 explosions. I don't understand those first two columns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I start with the first column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is DTG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Date, time, group. 18 is the date; then we have 0035 Bravo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does Bravo mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's local time. Zero time in military terms, the Greenwich time; Alpha time is normal time; Bravo time is summertime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, what time is 0035 Bravo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is 35 minutes after midnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then the happen something going from that to 0120 Bravo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's that? That is 20 past 1.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And SG-2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SG-2, it's the abbreviation of an OP or a team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now what does that SG mean? Can you tell us what SG stands for then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember, sir. If you go to the line 2, OP 4, it's observation post 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, I understand that. But I want to understand SG-2, and I want to understand SI-1, which is below OP 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's either an observation post or a team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And what does -- I can't see that. It's BP899610.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a six-figure map degree within 100 metres, within 100 metres accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I hope counsel understand what that means. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, much. Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in order to clarify a bit more, you keep saying there is a grid reference that's demoted by the BP followed by six numbers, did the observer teams and any other teams, did you have a standardised mapping system that you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. This is a standard military map: 1:50.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So when these grid references are being listed, it's off of a map, not the map that we were looking at previously, but a map that was unique to the UN post there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the maps that had been shown here, it's a map with the -- I call it standard military 1:50.000 map. Standard for every military and it's also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, just for purposes of clarification, and I certainly don't mean to interrupt your examination, Ms. Carter. My understanding is that the observation post was in a particular area and remained there, and that the BP863599, which is the grid number for OP 4 is the grid number where they always were located and that would be found on a particular grid map which we have yet to see on -- it is a static position to identify where the observation post was on a particular military map, on a particular kind of map where they show grid positions. I hope that is of some help.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Brennskag, can you confirm for the Court whether that read something accurate. Is the fixed position of observation post 4 at the grid reference 863599 that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That is the fixed positions of OP 4 on the hills over Vitkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now we also see in the impact and target area, there are also appear to be grid references, but they don't contain six digits, only four at times and then others are longer. What is the difference between a shorter grid reference and a longer grid reference?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: A four-numbered grid reference is within a square of 1.000 metre; a six-letter or numbered grid reference is within a square of 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Does that assist Your Honours, or should I go further with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, ma'am. Just carry on with your examining.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to move to page 8 of the same document. And just for clarification, I'd like to look at the registering of a single explosion at a 11.46 local time. And I want to confirm that your observation post registered a shot being fired from the Bosnian Serb side into Dobrinja at that time. Is that a correct reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get the witness read, Madam Carter, instead of you testifying? We don't know what are you looking at; 11.46 as I see it, the origin is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please explain on the six listings that you had indicated before, can you please explain what does the firing at 11.46 mean?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Could you please put the cursor on where you mean? Oh, yeah. We are still on the 18th and is stated that at 11.46 local time, it was observed from OP 4 one explosion from where, unknown, and the impact was in Dobrinja on the grid reference Bravo Papa, 865564. And in the explanation, it is stated that it fired from BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If you have a remark that that shot was being fired from the Bosnian Serb side, why is it listed as unknown about the origin of the fire?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's the procedure, because you couldn't -- or the OP, they couldn't specify the grid reference from where, but they could see that the fire came from the BSA-held side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution seeks to tender 65 ter 8594 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given exhibit P543. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At that point, Madam Carter, would that would be a convenient time for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was about to change topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in your earlier testimony you've made reference on a few occasions to modified air bombs, and I now want to turn your attention to those. Can you please tell the Court what is a modified air bomb, to the extent that you know?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. At first, I have to admit that I'm not an expert on modified air bombs. But I have learned that is a -- normally a ballistic missile, which is put on rocket device.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "a ballistic missile," what specifically does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. A ballistic missile get its power from the initial launching and not during its way to the target. If you put on a rocket device, it can bring the missile longer and take it out of the ballistic movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You have indicated the ballistic missile gets its power from initial launching. Are any of the other items that we've discussed here in court today considered missiles? You discussed mortars, you discussed artillery rounds. What is the nature of those items?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Those are ballistic missiles. A rifle bullet is also a ballistic missile. Got its power from the initial firing only.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. How many times did you encounter a modified air bomb in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's hard to say: 4, 5, 6, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And this is your personal experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. In your work with those certain instances, was there a certain location where these were fired from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can recall today, most of those air bomb, modified air bombs, were fired from the Ilidza area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who controlled Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was, at that time, BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the accuracy of modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It depends on the launcher and the accuracy of putting on the rocket devices. But normally those modified air bombs, they are not at all useful as a normally weapon in normal war. It's not accurate -- accurate enough. I can compare it maybe from the Middle East, where the -- and now at this times, from Gaza, the Katyusha rockets. They're not able to fire them to exact target.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your dealings with these modified air bombs, were you ever responsible for the investigation of such items?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I especially remember two times. I was together with colleagues to investigate impacts from modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you describe the first of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was not that far away from the PTT building on the other side of the main road going east to west in Sarajevo, in a place called Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, just so we're clear, Your Honour, if we could have a date. The reason because there are certain unscheduled incidents that should not be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly and the Prosecution is aware of that. And we will not be leading any detail to the reference that is being made.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify the date of the first encounter you had with the modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, I have my notes, and I think I correctly said it was the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now you began describing that investigation and you said that it was a place called Alipasino Polje. If you could please describe a bit further your investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm mistaken, but I do believe this is an unscheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The unscheduled incident is on 28 June 1995, and it will be not be led. Two investigations that this witness was part of do not entail that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying, Madam Carter, that the incident of the 22nd of June is a scheduled incident, the one that he is now talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's neither scheduled nor unscheduled. This is merely to show the wide-sped and systematic pattern as described in the decision of the Court of 31 October 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I tend to disagree. The decision speaks for itself. This is being used for an improper purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't remember the decision. What does the decision say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the decision was in relation to the objection made by Defence counsel that leading any evidence of incidents that are not scheduled would be in violation of the 73 bis decision. This Court determined in paragraph 11 of the same decision that the scheduled incidents listed in the indictment need to be read in conjunction with paragraphs 40 to 46 of the indictment; and that's specifically why this witness is being called, which refer to a protracted campaign of shelling and sniping upon Sarajevo, resulting in the killing and wounding of thousands of citizens -- I'm sorry, thousands of civilians. It follows that in order to prove these broad allegation, the Prosecution must be able to lead evidence of a general nature related to the shelling and sniping campaign against civilians outside of the incidents listed in schedules A and B of the indictment. So we're calling in relation to that specific purpose as opposed to any sort of scheduled or unscheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is grounds that we've been through before. Both incidents of the 22nd of June and one on July 1995 are mentioned in the 65 ter summary, which is what the Trial Chamber referred to in the paragraph above.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is -- which is this is -- that it is recognised by the Chamber; that this is it unscheduled incident. I'm referring specifically to the incident of the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Yes, Madam Carter, did say, yes, it is not scheduled. But she is saying that the decision said that the Prosecution is entitled to lead evidence on unscheduled incidents to show the widespread and systematic nature of the sniping or -- or of the attack. And I don't have the decision before me, so I can only rely on what she tells me, and I believe her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What she quoted from the decision is not -- is not inaccurate. Which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's not inaccurate, it must be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 10 of the decision, it states: "The Trial Chamber, therefore, agrees with the submission of the Prosecution that the words 'unscheduled incidents' as stated in Rule 73 bis decision refers to unscheduled incidents described as such in the 65 ter witness summaries." It continues, but that is the point that is of importance. The Chamber then holds, and I go down to paragraph 15, under disposition: "For the forgoing reasons and pursuant to Rules 54 of the rules, the Trial Chamber decides that the term 'unscheduled incidents' in the Rule 73 bis decision shall be interpreted as those unscheduled incidents as such in the Prosecution's 65 ter witness summaries." And this is an incident which is described in the 65 ter witness summary. Because it is described in the 65 ter witness summary which is not the situation we have been in with other incidents it falls within this prohibition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Within which prohibition? You say for the foregoing reasons and pursuant to Rule 54 of the rules, the Trial Chamber decides that the term unscheduled incidents in the Rule 73 bis decision shall be interpreted as those unscheduled incidents as such in the Prosecution's 65 ter witness summaries. Now, how do you read this paragraph in?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have previously been in the situation where the Prosecution has led unscheduled incidents which are not contained in the 65 ter summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as to those incidents, the Chamber -- the Chamber, over objection, made the determination because they were not in the 65 ter summaries they were incidents which, in fact, could be led. It has been our interpretation that based upon this decision although we had some difficulty what was said before by virtue of the underlying decision that we have been fighting with regard to unscheduled incidents in the first instance, that where the Prosecution has identified an incident in a 65 ter summary, which is unscheduled, it is not to be led.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could be allowed to respond to for clarity for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith indications regards to that rule, he is correct. However, in the 65 ter summary of Brennskag, it falls into three categories. The first paragraph is noted as just basically biographical information; it doesn't have any sort of heading. The second is a shelling and artillery fire; that is what we are we're discussing here, and it reads, I quote: "The witness will speak about use of modified air bombs by the VRS. He will testify that he saw four or five modified air bombs," and we go on from there which is the evidence being led. The third category in the 65 ter summary indicates unscheduled shelling incident, the TV building incident of 28 June 1995. This Court, in its decision of 31 October 2008, specifically identified that those items that are listed as unscheduled incidents, in this case, the 28 June 1995, cannot be led before the Court; and we certainly have no intention of doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Talk to the 22nd of June, ma'am, what is the status of the 22nd of June incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The 22nd June incident falls under the category shelling and artillery. It has not been denoted as an unscheduled incident in violation of the Court's 73 bis order; so we are talking about apples and oranges here. We are not leading the evidence that has been specifically prohibited by the 31 October decision, but we are leading evidence in regards to shelling and artillery fire to show the widespread and systematic shelling of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me -- excuse me, Your Honour. I think quite frankly the Prosecution is playing word games to put it simply. Schedule A of the indictment contains nine incidents. Those incidents do not include the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They do include the 1st of July, which is another incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, the 1st of July incident would be a scheduled incident that they can lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There will be absolutely not objection, and I will not be rising with regard to that incident. With regard to the 22nd of June, it is an unscheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But then Madam Carter read a paragraph -- the very first paragraph she read, she said that -- she said that they -- she read something to the effect that the Chamber holds -- okay, let me have a look at it. What paragraph was that? The first paragraph that you read, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Out of the decision, Your Honour, that would be paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, now we're moving back to your investigation of 22 June of -- I'm sorry, of 1995. As much time has passed, if you can begin your description again: What was the incident that you investigated on 22 June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was an incident of an impact in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did you become aware of the incident?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Normally I was not at the observation post, so the team was called from UN HQ, told us about the incident, approximately the map grid, and gave us order to investigate the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did you find when you arrived on site?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was just in Alipasino Polje. It's very high buildings. And outside one of the buildings, it's - what you call it - tarmac road, paved road, and the rocket or grenade has landed on the paved road; and it was one young, very young girl who was killed. When we arrived, almost simultaneously the Bosnian police investigation team also arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let me clarify just one moment. Now, you have indicated that this was a rocket or grenade. Is it a rocket, a grenade, or modified air bomb that's at issue?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: When we started the investigation, it was fairly soon clear that this was a sort of modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And what was your role in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Me and my colleague was to clarify the direction from where the projectile was fired and to see how -- which -- what kind of projectile, and also to testify what was the impact of the incident, wounded, killed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that it was you and your colleague's job to clarify the direction from where the projectile was fired. Were you able to determine that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. It's a certain method to find from where, but it's difficult to -- to find exact place of firing, of course, how far the distance, especially when it's not a -- especially when it's a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you have any indication that it was fired by the Bosnian side, the Bosnian Serb side, or a third party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, I think that's a very leading question. Why don't you ask the witness to tell you where it came from, according to his determination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, where did the air bomb come from, according to your determination?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At the spot we couldn't decide, but together with other observations, not from me because I was not on the OP, the UN observer HQ as far as I know today determined that this was coming from BSA-held side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And now I would like to move to the second investigation that were a part of on 1 July, 1995. Can you please describe that investigation?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We were called on, as the same procedure. This time it was a modified air bomb landing in a garden. It's -- I don't remember the name, because it is very difficult. But it's a little bit north of the main road going east -- west-east in Sarajevo and just east of -- of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did you find when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Huge crater, and the building that belongs to the garden or were damaged, especially the -- the roof and the windows. The Sarajevan police also arrived, and we were soon clarifying there were no injured and no killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up 65 ter 1365.01.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the image before you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, that's the spot. That's the building. That's the roof damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 1365.01 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P544.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now like to bring up the image 65 ter 1365.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same place. I see the ladder. I don't see the house. And I see not a good picture of the crater behind the first tree, between the first tree, I see and the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, were there any military targets anywhere near this house?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but as far as I know, there were no military positions there. That's -- I say I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would seek to tender 65 ter 1365 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the last question that I have for you is: Which sides of this conflict were in possession of modified air bombs, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the BSA had in their possessions and possibility to use modified air bombs. In my knowledge, I have never seen and never heard that the ABiH inside Sarajevo was in possession of this kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I thank you for your time and your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I seek to pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have P542 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While it's coming up. Good morning, sir. How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if that could be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You testified that this map identifies, if I'm not mistaken, two separate places, one where there's a triangle and the letter 4, which was your observation post; and the second being where you were, I take it, either billeted or working when you were not at the observation post; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, the circle was the accommodation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you were to -- I have a quick question for the -- for the Madam Registrar, if we are to make a new mark on this now, can we give it a new number? Perfect. Looking at this particular map, on this map, close to your observation post, there was a T-55 tank that was being utilised by the ABiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's correct. On our way to the OP, we could see, observe, the T55 tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the help of Mr. Usher, if could you mark the location of the T-55 tank, using the colour red, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: My memory is -- but it should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark that circle with the letter T and the numbers 55.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now apart from the T-55, which you have noted on the map, looking at this particular area, do you, as you sit here today, recall any of the other areas that were army installations of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean. I knew several places where they had their offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you, once again, using the red, mark the first of those areas where you knew they had their offices.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall because it was several places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you mark, as you're looking at the map, any of the areas where you recall that they had headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was a headquarters somewhere in a building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark that with a "ABiH 1," please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from that area, do you recall since you mentioned there were several, do you recall any other areas where you, in your capacity as an UNMO observer saw ABiH facilities?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I knew they had mortars in an area where there was car wreckage. I'm not sure exactly where it was, but it was somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you mark the area that you have just designated with a circle with the letter "ABiH M," for "mortars."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from those two areas, as you sit here today, do you recall any other places where there were ABiH facilities or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In all respect, it would be too -- it would be to speculate because it's too long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, I don't want you to speculate. As you sit here today, and as you look at that particular document, could you tell the Chamber to the best of your recollection - I don't want you to draw anything - how many other ABiH facilities you recall being observing during the period of time that you were stationed at observation post 4? How many, as opposed to why they were?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Excuse me, do you mean offices or positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's do offices first.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can remember, I was in a meeting on two offices. But I can't recall exactly where they were. Some were here. It was an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you mark with the red pen an approximate area since that --

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That is very approximate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the letters "ABiH 3."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said there were two offices. Did you go to two offices in the same location, or was there another location that you also met?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yeah, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Apart from the offices, you mentioned the issue of positions; and independent of the question of confrontation lines which have you been kind enough to supply us with in a previous map, when you were using the term positions are you meaning something apart from the designation of where the confrontation lines were?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. I can recall the position of the mortars, as I have marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In addition to the position of the mortars, do you recall any other positions that the ABiH had that you could mark on this particular map during the time that you were at OP 4?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have that marked as -- moved into evidence as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have mentioned that your movement was restricted by the ABiH, in terms of areas where you could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have -- I believe it's 541, I think is the -- P541, I believe, is the original unmarked, up on the screen, please. I'm sorry, it's 540. Thank you, Chad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that map to come up, when you were receiving your training with regard to observations, were you at any point in time given as calculations to use either the speed of sound or the speed of light, in terms of how fast the speed of sound is, or the speed of light is?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of trying to make a determination of origin of fire or origin of impact, were you ever supplied the actual speed of sound, as a mechanical formula, a mathematical formula that could you use for purposes of determining where something came from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. We didn't have that devices as observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the speed of sound -- I'm sorry, with regard to the speed of light, were you ever given the mathematical formula of the speed of light as something to utilise as an observer, in terms of the point of origin or the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever receive any information as an observer with regard to the speed that a mortar shell would travel?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Not at that time, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, same question with regard to air bombs. Were you given any information concerning the -- the calculated speed with which an air bomb travelled?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I was not given that information in -- during my time in Sarajevo, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you given any information with regard to trajectory paths as a general rule, with regard to, first of all, mortars in -- in an attempt to assist you with regard to your job as an observer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That was a knowledge that I had as officer from the Norwegian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that knowledge which you all shared with each other? Did you have a chart or some kind of other document that assisted you with regard to trajectories and arcs and the like?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I -- in -- as -- in my remembering, I think the UN gave us a pamphlet of some information. But I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. As you sit here today, you have some memory about that, but you're not positive about that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of, once again, trajectory paths, were you supplied with any information concerning the arc of trajectory as a related to the distance from which a particular projectile was fired?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. If I understand you correctly, regarding ballistic missiles, during the time we were investigating an impact, the metal, the angle of the impact could tell us approximately from where and the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the -- the angle of impact could indicate the distance of the trajectory?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: When it was a ballistic missile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see that the map is up on the screen now, so I'd like to direct your attention to the map. Looking at that map, and I know it is it kind of small, so if it's a bit small we can perhaps try to enlarge it. But, first of all, looking at the map as it sits there right now, are you able to identify any of the areas that you were not allowed to go into by the ABiH since you indicated they restricted your movement?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. For me it's easy because you are rejected to go to any places near the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With the help of the usher then. Once again, using the red pen, could you mark on this document those areas that you were not allowed to go to by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In all respect, I made briefly a drawing of the confrontation line, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would that be helpful to you, in terms of what I have just asked you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As I said, we were rejected to go anywhere near or close to the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I believe the confrontation line was -- map was P541.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've used the term -- the map will come newspaper a moment. You used the term "near," and since that term is potentially one which is relative, as you're looking at this map right now, where have you drawn the confrontation lines, can you indicate how close you were allowed to get to the confrontation line, in terms of metres or kilometres, first of all, before we place any marks on the map? Could you tell us about how far you could go?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]
