utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see you have drawn what seems to be a -- ah. You have drawn an arrow which is bisecting a line.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Sorry, and it's approximate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say that the areas that -- the area that is before the -- the straight line that you have drawn is the area in which you were allowed to go and anything outside of that is an area where you were not allowed to go. So you could actually draw a circle, if you were to draw a circle around that whole area, would that be a fair representation of those areas where you were not allowed to go?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Could you put somewhere the following two words, "no go" on the map?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry could we have that -- could we have that admitted as defendant's next in order, Your Honour. I'm sorry my voice dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't need that anymore. Thank you. If we could now have P543. I will be next asking for P543 and page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that come up, sir, you mentioned the Famos factory in your testimony. Could you tell us if you know what was being manufactured at the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you, as a matter of practice, have daily discussions with the other UNMOs who were at other observation points, so that you all kept each other abreast of what was going on, independent of the radio traffic that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Not regularly, but we had -- the team leaders had meetings in the HQ on regular basis and passed on the informations after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And some of the information that was passed on; for example, the troop strength of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time receive information as to what the troop strength of the ABiH was during the time that you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Do you mean the entire ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I mean those people who were billeted and fighting in the area in which you were observing.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, I didn't get any exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you get guesstimate figures from any intelligence sources at all?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have page 8 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had been asked a question about the time of 11.46 Bravo, and I'd like to talk to you about a number of entries that are on this page to see whether or not we can make some sense of what was occurring. If we are to start at the time of, let's say, 10.50 Bravo, which is an entry of OP 4. It indicate there is two explosions; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then 23 minutes later, there is another entry; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Which time?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I don't see the whole screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. If you were to look -- if you were to look on -- it's five lines down. It says 1113 Bravo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's another explosion; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, between 11.30 and 12.15 there seem to be a number of outgoing mortar rounds; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It seems to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the entry of 11.46 that you have noted is -- is an entry that occurs during the period of time that there's firing between 11.30 and 12.15 outgoing BiH fire; right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we continue to go down, there are seen a series of what I'm assuming, based on this, are unknown firings between 11.46 and 12.01; and it seems then if we continue down we have entries at 11.49, 12.15, 12.50, 13.05, 13.00 and 13.00 to 13.15. So there seems to be -- if we go even further, but it seems what's going on there is a battle. I'm asking because it seems there is firing coming in and there's firing going out?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's a kind of thing that you were talking about before, when you said there were rounds that you observed coming in and there are rounds that you observed going out. With regard to the mortars that were going out, could you tell the Chamber what size they were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, what size of mortar was it that was being used by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Let me clarify the date of 18th, I'm not sure if I was on the observation post. But mostly, as a general, I know that the outgoing mortars was around 80 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you said you were not on the observation post, if you had been on the observation post, were you able to visually make a determination of a size of the a mortar shell by seeing it launched or in the air?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, not seeing it launched in the area. But as I said, we were aware of mortars positions for ABiH in a junkyard for cars. And by the sound of outgoing, we could estimate it was around 80-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that training you received - and by training I don't mean school training but, rather, experience that you obtained while observing that the sound of an 80-millimetre was distinct from the sound of, let's say, for example, a 50-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, estimate was by experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did your unit in OP 4 file a report every day?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't tell what my colleagues did. But normally, when I was there, we filed the incidents we were observing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it just as important to recognise and to note a date where there was no activity as a date where there was activity for purposes of monitoring what was occurring?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was not important to -- to file if nothing happened. We filed the incidents and what was happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of cease-fire, did anybody at headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are we okay or are we having some trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You go ahead while we sort ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did anybody at headquarters indicate to you, your unit that it was important to know when there was not any mortar activity, because it would indicate that the cease-fire was holding?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand you right, but if no reports, either by radio or afterwards by written, there was nothing to -- there were no incidents and no firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But what I'm asking, is was there a methodology to -- with regard to your unit, was there a methodology whereby headquarters would be aware of the fact that they had a successful day. There'd been no firing which they then noted down somewhere. All of the observation post report in, Hey good day, no firing. The cease-fires is holding. Because that was just as important as when it wasn't; right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's obvious when no reports, either by radio or written statements, no firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I understand, the practice of the United Nations, with regard to observations was, as follows: If no reports were entered, it was a day of peace?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned - if I'm not mistaken - fortunately you were out of Sarajevo, or maybe it was Pale, on 24th of May, and that all of your colleagues had been seized or detained.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I went out to Pale early morning, the 24th of May, and it was -- and all my colleagues were detained except of the team leader who was on leave earlier and was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And were all of your colleagues detained in response to something that had happened?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I think the 25th or 26th of May, NATO first air-strike on BSA ammunition bunkers took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And were -- to your knowledge, were your colleagues detained before the NATO strike?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Afterwards. They were detained nearby ammunition bunkers and so on, to -- obviously to -- in order that the NATO would not go further with the air-strike. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did your colleagues at some point get released?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I think the last of my colleagues in my team in Pale was released 19th of June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And are you personally aware of who participated in effectuating the release of your colleagues? And by that, I mean were you aware of the negotiations that occurred at higher levels in attempt to get your colleagues, and ultimately to get your colleagues released.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was on high level in the UN and high level on the BSA authorities or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know who ordered the detention of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from the BSA authorities, do you have any personal knowledge - which all I'm asking for here - of any other authorities apart from the BSA authorities being involved in the negotiation of the successful release of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Not as I remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have but a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank goodness for those about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of mortars once again, and by that I'm referring to the ABiH army mortar, were you aware of any mortars being moved from one position to another position during the time that you were an observer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We knew that, and also of experience, that when you are firing a mortar round, or mortars, you move to another position. We were aware of that -- the ABiH did so also, but I didn't see with my bare eyes those movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would the movement by the ABiH of their mortar position have been something that would have been transmitted over the radio before you decided to have radio silence concerning mortar issues. So by that what I mean is within -- within UNMO, if mortars were moved from position 1 to 2 by the ABiH, is that something that would have gone on over the radio so that the observers would be in a position to know where to focus their sight lines with regard to either incoming or outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In my time as observer, I never heard radio communication about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your time as an observer, did you receive any documentary evidence concerning that matter; a written report, for example?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. A British unit with devices to spot the mortar velocity, height, and so on with the rounds were posted not as far -- not far from our OP, and once we saw a sketch declaring from where it has been fired, the impacts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that sketch made part of your daily report?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, this was purely occasionally because we once visited this unit. We didn't see this report regularly. I don't know if the HQ had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was the British unit that you're referring to an UNPROFOR unit as opposed to an UNMO units?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: UNPROFOR unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did you share information with UNPROFOR regarding incoming and outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That was the matter of the HQ in PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to your own personal experience, did you personally obtain any information from UNPROFOR to assist you in your job as an observer? And by "assist you," I'm referring to such issues as mortar placement and mortar movement.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: In my time as observer inside Sarajevo, I -- we had assistance from UNPROFOR, but I can't recognise that we got that kind of information or assistance, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have a very brief redirect on two topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The first one, you were asked today at page 39 about seeing a T-55 tank near your observation post "utilised," was the word that was used. Did you ever see in your time at OP 4 that tank ever fire?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, not at all. It looks like it was abandoned. But I didn't see or hear anything that could tell me that it was firing from that tank, and it was never moved, as far as I was travelling to and fro OP 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The final topic I'd like to discuss with you is you were asked, beginning on page 43 about the information you received and how you were tracking or had the possibility of tracking the trajectory or the origin of fire or origin of impact of the missiles that you were seeing there in Sarajevo; so I want to focus your attention to that. First off, if you hadn't received the items listed by Mr. Smith, what did you use in order to determine the origin of fire or the origin of impact?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Normally, on some places, we saw the origin of fire. Actually, in the east of Sarajevo, we could, from our OP see the artillery positions of the BSA. We could hear the firing. Sometimes we only heard and saw the impact, and then we couldn't say the origin of firing. They were firing with heavy machine-guns and also anti-aircraft guns towards Igman and the Igman road; and they use ammunition that have a light during the trajectory, so we could see the origin of firing, and we could see the impact. The modified air bombs, we could see the smoke tail from the origin of firing and almost halfway, all the way to the target or to the impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your answer you used the term "they"; specifically that "they were firing." Can you please tell me who "they" is?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly this was from BSA-held areas, and we, as I tried to explain, especially one place we could see by our binoculars the artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and return at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lieutenant, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for taking the time to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution does not have another witness for today. The next witness will be available Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. In that event -- on Wednesday morning. We will stand adjourned until Wednesday morning, at 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom I. Court adjourned.
